{{Short description|Procedure to assess the quality of clinical trials}}
The '''Jadad scale''', sometimes known as '''Jadad scoring''' or the '''Oxford quality scoring system''', is a procedure to assess the methodological quality of a [[clinical trial]] by objective criteria. It is named after [[Canadian]]-[[Colombia]]n physician [[Alex Jadad]] who in 1996 described a system for allocating such trials a score of between zero (very poor) and five (rigorous). It is the most widely used such assessment in the world, and as of May 2024, its seminal paper has been cited in over 25,000 scientific works.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?view_op=view_citation&hl=en&user=pjha-gkAAAAJ&citation_for_view=pjha-gkAAAAJ:_xSYboBqXhAC| title = Assessing the quality of reports of randomized clinical trials: is blinding necessary?| website = Google Scholar| access-date = 11 May 2024}}</ref>

==Description==
The Jadad scale independently assesses the methodological quality of a [[clinical trial]] judging the [[unblinding|effectiveness of blinding]]. [[Alex Jadad|Alejandro "Alex" Jadad Bechara]], a Colombian physician who worked as a Research Fellow at the Oxford Pain Relief Unit, Nuffield Department of Anaesthetics at the [[University of Oxford]] described the allocating trials a score of between zero (very poor) and five (rigorous) in an appendix to a 1996 paper.<ref name="jadad">{{cite journal| last= Jadad | first= A.R. | authorlink=Alex Jadad|author2=Moore R.A. |author3=Carroll D. |author4=Jenkinson C. |author5=Reynolds D.J.M. |author6=Gavaghan D.J. |author7=McQuay H.J.  | title= Assessing the quality of reports of randomized clinical trials: Is blinding necessary? |journal= Controlled Clinical Trials|volume=17 |issue=1 |pages= 1–12| doi= 10.1016/0197-2456(95)00134-4| year= 1996 | pmid=8721797}}</ref>
In a 2007 book, Jadad described the randomised controlled trial as "one of the simplest, most powerful and revolutionary forms of research".<ref>{{cite book|last=Jadad|first=Alejandro R.|author2=Enkin, Murray |title=Randomized Controlled Trials: Questions, Answers and Musings| publisher=Blackwell| year=2007| edition=2nd| isbn=978-1-4051-3266-4}}</ref>

==Background==
{{main|Randomised controlled trial}}
Clinical trials are conducted for the purpose of collecting data on the efficacy of medical treatments.<ref name=chow>{{cite book|last=Chow|first=Shein-Chung|author2=Liu, Jen-pei|title=Design and Analysis of Clinical Trials|publisher=Wiley|year=2004|page=2|isbn=978-0-471-24985-6|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HXMUEjZ4vyAC&pg=PA2}}</ref> The treatment might be, for example, a new [[drug]], a [[medical device]], a [[surgical procedure]], or a preventative regime.<ref name=chow/> [[Clinical trial protocol]]s vary considerably depending on the nature of the treatment under investigation,<ref>{{cite book|last=Brian |first=Everitt|author2=Pickles, Andrew|title=Statistical Aspects of the Design and Analysis of Clinical Trials|publisher=Imperial College Press|year=2004|page=5|isbn=978-1-86094-441-3|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=DMiH5y6SDuQC}}</ref> but typically, in a controlled trial, researchers gather a group of volunteers and subject some to the test treatment, while giving the others either no treatment (known as a [[placebo]]) or an established treatment for comparison. After a defined time period, the patients in the test group are assessed for health improvements in comparison with the [[control group]].{{cn|date=November 2023}}

However, trials can vary greatly in quality. Methodological errors such as poor [[Blind experiment|blinding]] or poor [[randomisation]] allow factors such as the [[placebo effect]] or [[selection bias]] to adversely affect the results of a trial.<ref name="Colditz">{{cite journal|last=Colditz|first=G.A.|author2=Miller J.N. |author3=Mosteller F. |year=1989|title=How study design affects outcomes in comparisons of therapy|journal=Statistics in Medicine | volume=8|issue=4|pages=441–454|doi=10.1002/sim.4780080408 | pmid = 2727468 }}</ref>

===Randomisation===
Randomisation is a process to remove potential distortion of statistical results arising from the manner in which the
trial is conducted, in particular in the selection of subjects. Studies have indicated, for example, that nonrandomised trials are more likely to show a positive result for a new treatment than for an established conventional one.<ref name="Colditz"/>

===Blinding===
{{main article|Blind experiment}}
The importance of [[scientific control]]s to limit factors under test is well established. However, it is also important that none of those involved in a clinical trial, whether the researcher, the subject patient or any other involved parties, should allow their own prior expectations to affect reporting of results.<ref name="Day">{{cite journal|last=Day|first=Simon J |author2=Altman, Douglas G |title=Blinding in clinical trials and other studies|journal=British Medical Journal|volume=321|issue=7259|page=504|url= |pmid=10948038|year=2000|pmc=1118396|doi=10.1136/bmj.321.7259.504}}</ref> The [[placebo effect]] is known to be a confounding factor in trials; affecting the ability of both patients and doctors to report accurately on the clinical outcome. [[Blind experiment|Experimental blinding]] is a process to prevent [[bias]], both conscious and subconscious, skewing results.<ref name="Day"/>

Blinding frequently takes the form of a [[placebo]], an inactive dummy that is indistinguishable from the real treatment. Blinding can however be difficult to achieve in some trials,<ref name="Day" /> for example, [[surgery]] or [[physical therapy]]. Poor blinding can exaggerate the perceived effects of treatment, particularly if any such effects are small.<ref>{{cite journal | title=The revised CONSORT statement for reporting randomized trials: explanation and elaboration | journal=Annals of Internal Medicine | date=2001-04-17 | first1=DG | last1=Altman | first2=KF|last2=Schulz|first3=D|last3=Moher|first4=M|last4=Egger|first5=F|last5=Davidoff|first6=D|last6=Elbourne|first7=PC|last7=Gøtzsche|first8=T|last8=Lang|last9=CONSORT GROUP (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) | volume=134 | issue=8 |pages=663–694 | pmid=11304107 | doi=10.7326/0003-4819-134-8-200104170-00012 | s2cid=12834600 }}</ref> Blinding should be appropriate to the study, and is ideally [[double blind]], wherein neither the patient nor doctor is aware of whether they are in the control or test group, eliminating any such psychological effects from the study.{{cn|date=November 2023}}

===Withdrawals and dropouts===
Withdrawals and [[dropping out|dropouts]] are those patients who fail to complete a course of treatment, or fail to report back on its outcome to the researchers. The reasons for doing so might be varied: the individuals may have moved away, abandoned the course of treatment, or died. Whatever the reason, the attrition rate can skew results of a study, particularly for those subjects who ceased treatment due to perceived inefficacy. In [[smoking cessation]] studies, for example, it is routine to consider all dropouts as failures.<ref>
{{cite conference

==Jadad questionnaire==
A three-point questionnaire forms the basis for a Jadad score.<ref name="jadad"/> Each question was to be answered with either a ''yes'' or a ''no''. Each ''yes'' would score a single point, each ''no'' zero points; there were to be no fractional points. The Jadad team stated that they expected it should take no longer than ten minutes to score any individual paper. The questions were as follows: ''Was the study described as randomized?'',  ''Was the study described as double blind?'' and ''Was there a description of withdrawals and dropouts?''<ref name="jadad"/>

To receive the corresponding point, an article should describe the number of withdrawals and dropouts in each of the study groups, and the underlying reasons. Additional points were given if: ''The method of randomisation was described in the paper, and that method was appropriate.'' or ''The method of blinding was described, and it was appropriate.''<ref name="jadad"/>

Points would be ''deducted'' if: ''The method of randomisation was described, but was inappropriate'', or ''The method of blinding was described, but was inappropriate.''<ref name="jadad"/>

A clinical trial could therefore receive a Jadad score of between zero and five. The Jadad scale is sometimes described as a five-point scale, though there are only three questions.

==Uses==
The Jadad score may be used in a number of ways:

# To evaluate the general quality of medical research in a particular field.<ref name="Acupuncture">{{cite book|last=White|first=Adrian|author2=Ernst, Edzard|title=Acupuncture: A Scientific Appraisal|publisher=Elsevier |year=1999|page=109|isbn=978-0-7506-4163-0|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e2KkvlQI7sYC&pg=PA109}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Wang|first=Gang|title=The quality of reporting of randomized controlled trials of traditional Chinese medicine|journal=Clinical Therapeutics|volume=29|issue=7|pages=1456–1467|doi=10.1016/j.clinthera.2007.07.023|year=2007|pmid=17825697|display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Welk|first=B.|author2=Afshar, K. |author3=MacNeily, A.E. |title=Randomized controlled trials in pediatric urology: room for improvement|journal=J Urol|volume=176|issue=1|pages=306–310|doi=10.1016/S0022-5347(06)00560-X|year=2006|pmid=16753430}}</ref>
# To set a minimum standard for the paper's results to be included in a [[meta analysis]]. A researcher conducting a [[systematic review]] for example might elect to exclude all papers on the topic with a Jadad score of 3 or less.<ref>{{cite book|last=Simon|first=Stephen D. |title=Statistical Evidence in Medical Trials: What Do the Data Really Tell Us?|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2006|page=122|isbn=978-0-19-856761-5|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zaq99M2p_sEC&pg=PA121}}</ref>
# For critical analysis of an individual paper.

{{as of| 2008}}, the Jadad score was the most widely used such assessment in the world,<ref name="Clinical Epidemiology">{{cite book|last1=Hayes|first1=R.B.|last2=Sackett|first2=D.L.|last3=Guyatt|first3=G.H.|last4=Tugwell|first4=P.|title=Clinical Epidemiology|publisher=Lippincott Williams & Wilkins|year=2005|page=31|isbn=978-0-7817-4524-6|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cuvY6TItIwgC&pg=PA31}}</ref><ref name="scales">{{cite journal|last=Olivo |first=SA|author2=Macedo LG |author3=Gadotti IC |author4=Fuentes J |author5=Stanton T |author6=Magee DJ |year=2008|title=Scales to Assess the Quality of Randomized Controlled Trials : A Systematic Review|journal=Physical Therapy|volume=88|issue=2|issn=0031-9023 |doi=10.2522/ptj.20070147|pages=156–75|pmid=18073267|doi-access=free}}</ref> and its seminal paper has been cited in over 3000 scientific works.

==Criticism==
Critics have charged that the Jadad scale is flawed, being over-simplistic and placing too much emphasis on blinding,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Berger|first=V. W.|title=Is the Jadad Score the Proper Evaluation of Trials?|journal=[[J. Rheumatol.]]|year=2006|volume=33|issue=8|pages=1710–1712|pmid=16881132|issn=0315-162X|url=http://www.jrheum.com/subscribers/06/08/1710-c.html|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20080220154705/http://www.jrheum.com/subscribers/06/08/1710-c.html|archivedate=2008-02-20}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.imbi.uni-freiburg.de/OJS/cca/index.php/cca/article/view/5053|title=Systematic Review of Quality Assessment Instruments for Randomized Control Trials|publisher=The Cochrane Collaboration|accessdate=2008-11-12}}</ref> and can show low consistency between different raters.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Clark |first=H.D.|date=Oct 1999|title=Assessing the quality of randomized trials: reliability of the Jadad scale|pages=448–52|journal=[[Controlled Clinical Trials]]|volume=20|issue=5 | pmid = 10503804|doi=10.1016/S0197-2456(99)00026-4|display-authors=etal}}</ref> Furthermore, it does not take into account [[allocation concealment]], viewed by [[Cochrane (organisation)|The Cochrane Collaboration]] as paramount to avoid bias.<ref>Higgins JPT, Altman DG, Sterne JAC (editors). Chapter 8: Assessing risk of bias in included studies. In: Higgins JPT, Green S (editors). Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions Version 5.1.0 (updated March 2011). The Cochrane Collaboration, 2011. Available from www.cochrane-handbook.org.</ref>
